meta.title: Icelandic A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Icelandic → English (see the Icelandic, recall the meaning) and English → Icelandic (see an English meaning, recall the Icelandic). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words of Icelandic for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded word list for Icelandic as a foreign language was found published, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 354 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and little words every sentence is built out of — and the other 146 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Icelandic, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Icelandic has no word for 'a', so the 176 nouns carry their gender beside their meaning — masculine, feminine or neuter, which decides every ending the noun and its adjective take — and show the forms a dictionary gives a noun by: the definite (the article is an ending: hesturinn, 'the horse'), the genitive singular and the plural (hests, hestar); behind the All forms fold are its four cases, nominative, accusative, dative and genitive, in both numbers. The 106 verbs show their present 'he' form, past and supine (fer, fór, farið — the forms an Icelandic verb is learnt by), and behind the fold the present in all six persons, the past plural, the past participle and the imperative. Adjectives show their three genders and their comparison. Real example sentences come with 491 of the 500 words, three apiece for 473 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and the forms of nouns, adjectives and pronouns, and the past and supine of verbs: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). The present tense and imperative of verbs: The Database of Icelandic Morphology (Beygingarlýsing íslensks nútímamáls). The Árni Magnússon Institute for Icelandic Studies. Author and editor Kristín Bjarnadóttir. https://bin.arnastofnun.is (CC BY-SA 4.0) — six present forms and the imperative are taken for each verb, unchanged; nothing else is used. Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0), whose mis-encoded letters (đ for ð, ū for þ) were mapped back before counting. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
